changes.before:
Coaching helps a person build their own ability to do the work. FEMA's leadership course, IS-240 Leadership and Influence, describes a coaching leader as someone who trusts that people will do well with the right training and support. That leader offers support, encouragement and constructive feedback while the person carries the work. Coaching is one of several conversations a leader holds. Directing says what needs to happen and by when. Correcting names a problem with the work and what must change. A formal performance process, such as a documented performance concern or discipline, runs through Human Resources and, where a labor agreement applies, labor relations.

Coaching works best when the person chooses to take part. The U.S. Office of Personnel Management's 2018 memo on coaching says coaching is for learning and development and needs the voluntary participation of the person coached. It adds that coaching should not be a mandatory requirement for poor performance or a stand-in for a supervisor's performance management duties. That is federal guidance, not Minnesota policy. The reasoning still travels well. If coaching turns into a quiet warning, people soon learn to stop being honest in it.

Say which conversation you are starting. A sentence such as "I'd like to talk about how you want to grow in this work, and this isn't about a performance concern" lets the person relax and think. If it is a correction, say that too, kindly and plainly. Then hold the conversation with a shared-learning mindset, which FEMA's format names as part of setting the stage. Give full attention, invite dialogue and expect to learn something yourself. You may know more about the task. You do not know how the work looks from their seat, or what barrier they have already met.

Ask what you treat as the normal way to do the work. Much of what gets called a skill gap is a difference in style. Someone writes longer reports, speaks less in meetings, asks more questions or reaches the answer by a different route. Before you coach, ask whether the issue affects results for people served or for colleagues. Or is it a way of working you learned and happen to prefer? Then notice a second pattern on your team: who usually hears "let's talk it through," and who usually hears "this needs fixing." The last lesson returns to that question.

changes.before:
A simple format makes coaching easier to hold. The format here is adapted from the coaching steps in FEMA's IS-240 Leadership and Influence materials, which begin by setting the stage. This version has five steps: define the issue together, create a growth atmosphere, explore options together, agree on a plan, and follow up. FEMA wrote it for emergency management. The steps fit human services well, because so much of the work depends on judgment rather than fixed procedure. You will not always move through the steps in order, and that is fine.

Define the issue together before anyone offers a fix. FEMA's format asks the coach to be specific and clear about their own assumptions. Say what you have noticed and why it matters for the work, then ask how the other person sees it. The issue may turn out to be different from what you thought. A program consultant who seems slow to answer lead agencies may be waiting on guidance that never came. Put the goal in terms of the work, such as "lead agencies get a clear answer within the week," rather than "be more responsive."

Create a growth atmosphere, then explore options together. Point to what is already working, say plainly that you are there to help, and invite ideas. FEMA's materials describe a balance between inquiry and advocacy. Inquiry means learning how the other person sees things without judging or arguing. Advocacy means offering your own view and the reasons behind it. FEMA's advice is inquiry first, then advocacy, and to stay open when your ideas are questioned. Let the other person name some of the options. Your ideas are welcome, but offer them as options rather than as the answer.

Agree on a plan, set a follow-up date and keep the door open. A good plan names one or two steps, the support you will give and when you will talk again. Ask the person to say the plan in their own words, and let them keep it. At the follow-up, ask what happened, what helped and what got in the way, including anything you did or did not do. Then decide together what to keep, change or stop. When the person asks you to just give them the answer, you can share your view and still ask what they think first.

changes.before:
Good coaching depends more on listening than on advice. FEMA's IS-242 Effective Communication course describes empathic listening as attending to thoughts, beliefs and feelings, not only to words. It describes paraphrasing as restating the main points in your own words, so the speaker can tell whether the message landed. FEMA suggests a paraphrase stay neutral, neither agreeing nor disagreeing. It also lists roadblocks to watch for in yourself, including hearing what you expect instead of what is said, hearing facts but not feelings, and stereotyping.

Open questions widen the other person's thinking. "What have you tried so far?" "What would a good result look like for the family?" "What would make this easier?" Each invites the person to reason. "Have you thought about calling the county?" is advice with a question mark at the end. It has its place, but use it after the person has had room to think. Ask one question at a time. Then leave a silence and let it do some work.

People show their thinking in different ways. Some think aloud and answer quickly. Some want time or prefer to write. Some learned that openly disagreeing with a supervisor is disrespectful. None of this tells you how capable someone is. The intercultural development continuum described by IDI, LLC can help you examine your coaching as a practice, never as a trait of any person. A Minimization habit sounds fair: I coach everyone the same way, the way that worked for me. An Acceptance habit notices that quick, direct questions suit some people and quiet others. An Adaptation habit changes the conversation, such as sending questions ahead, offering a written option or asking how the person likes to work through a problem. These names describe practices, never people.

Check whether your adaptation worked. At the end of a conversation, ask what was useful and what would make the next one easier. Notice whether the other person's ideas, not only yours, ended up in the plan. Never guess at someone's background or explain a style by culture. Ask how they like to work, and take the answer at face value. If a colleague mentions a non-visible disability, such as a hearing or processing difference, ask what helps. If they ask for a change at work because of a disability, treat that as an accommodation request: follow the agency's accommodation process with Human Resources or the ADA coordinator, and tell the person who decides. Look at your own defaults too. The style you treat as confident or capable was learned somewhere, and it shapes whom you see as ready.

It describes paraphrasing as restating the main points in your own words, so the speaker can tell whether the message landed. FEMA suggests a paraphrase stay neutral, neither agreeing nor disagreeing. It also lists roadblocks to watch for in yourself, including hearing what you expect instead of what is said, hearing facts but not feelings, and stereotyping.

Open questions widen the other person's thinking. "What have you tried so far?" "What would a good result look like for the family?" "What would make this easier?" Each invites the person to reason. "Have you thought about calling the county?" is advice with a question mark at the end. It has its place, but use it after the person has had room to think. Ask one question at a time. Then leave a silence and let it do some work.

People show their thinking in different ways. Some think aloud and answer quickly. Some want time or prefer to write. Some learned that openly disagreeing with a supervisor is disrespectful. None of this tells you how capable someone is. The following program illustrations borrow vocabulary from IDI, LLC’s intercultural development continuum to compare coaching approaches. They do not establish a person’s orientation. A Minimization habit sounds fair: I coach everyone the same way, the way that worked for me. An Acceptance habit notices that quick, direct questions suit some people and quiet others. An Adaptation habit changes the conversation, such as sending questions ahead, offering a written option or asking how the person likes to work through a problem. These names describe practices, never people.

Check whether your adaptation worked. At the end of a conversation, ask what was useful and what would make the next one easier. Notice whether the other person's ideas, not only yours, ended up in the plan. Never guess at someone's background or explain a style by culture. Ask how they like to work, and take the answer at face value. If a colleague mentions a non-visible disability, such as a hearing or processing difference, ask what helps. If they ask for a change at work because of a disability, treat that as an accommodation request: follow the agency's accommodation process with Human Resources or the ADA coordinator, and tell the person who decides. Look at your own defaults too. The style you treat as confident or capable was learned somewhere, and it shapes whom you see as ready.
changes.reason: Distinguish program illustrations from an assessment.

changes.before:
Who gets coached and who gets corrected is a pattern worth checking. Coaching is an investment of time, patience and the benefit of the doubt. When one person's rough draft gets "let's talk it through" and another's gets "this needs fixing by Friday," the first person is being developed and the second is being managed. Over time, that difference shapes who looks ready for the next opportunity. It rarely comes from bad intent. It often follows familiarity. People whose style or path resembles our own are easier to read as having potential.

Examine your own practice rather than other people. Think back over recent months without naming anyone or keeping a list. Which mistakes did you treat as learning, and which as problems? Did the same kind of mistake get a different response depending on who made it? Would you use the same words with someone else who did the same thing? If the answers are uneven, change the method. Offer coaching to everyone on a predictable basis. Use the same first question whenever work goes wrong: "What happened, and what do you need?"

Setbacks can be some of the best material for coaching. The Center for Creative Leadership's early research found that hardships were among the experiences leaders learned from. A 2020 CCL article reports that they were later dropped from the popular 70-20-10 guideline because organizations had little control over them. Treat it as a pointer from leadership research, not a rule. After a setback, ask what happened, what the person would do again, what they would do differently and what support was missing, including from you. Keep the talk on learning. Leave blame and repeated retelling out.

Some matters are not coaching matters. OPM's 2018 memo says coaching should not stand in for a supervisor's performance management duties. If work still falls short after support, talk with Human Resources about the performance process. Bring conduct, discipline and labor agreement questions to Human Resources and labor relations. Send concerns about discrimination, harassment or retaliation promptly to Human Resources or the equal opportunity office. Forward accommodation requests promptly under the agency's accommodation process, and tell the person who decides. Tell the person plainly that this part is now a different conversation. You can keep coaching on other goals.

Listening helps a coach understand the question before deciding what information or advice may help. FEMA's IS-242 Effective Communication course describes empathic listening as attending to thoughts, beliefs and feelings, not only to words. It describes paraphrasing as restating the main points in your own words, so the speaker can tell whether the message landed. FEMA suggests a paraphrase stay neutral, neither agreeing nor disagreeing. It also lists roadblocks to watch for in yourself, including hearing what you expect instead of what is said, hearing facts but not feelings, and stereotyping.

Open questions widen the other person's thinking. "What have you tried so far?" "What would a good result look like for the family?" "What would make this easier?" Each invites the person to reason. "Have you thought about calling the county?" is advice with a question mark at the end. It has its place, but use it after the person has had room to think. Ask one question at a time. Then leave a silence and let it do some work.

People may think aloud, prefer time to write, or hesitate to disagree with someone who supervises their work. Those observations do not establish capability or explain why a particular person responds that way. The following program illustrations borrow vocabulary from IDI, LLC’s intercultural development continuum to compare coaching approaches. They do not establish a person’s orientation. A Minimization habit sounds fair: I coach everyone the same way, the way that worked for me. An Acceptance habit notices that quick, direct questions suit some people and quiet others. An Adaptation habit changes the conversation, such as sending questions ahead, offering a written option or asking how the person likes to work through a problem. Use these examples to examine your approach, not to label a colleague.

changes.reason: Connect the explanation of communication preferences without inferring capability or cause.

Who gets coached and who gets corrected is a pattern worth checking. Coaching is an investment of time, patience and the benefit of the doubt. Different responses to similar work can affect access to development. Compare the work requirements, support offered and relevant circumstances before deciding whether the difference is justified. Familiarity may influence a judgment, but an uneven response alone does not establish why it happened. Direction and development can both be appropriate; the question is whether people have fair access to support.

Examine your own practice rather than other people. For this private learning reflection, consider recent months without putting names or personnel details in the exercise. This does not replace records required by your role. Which mistakes did you treat as learning, and which as problems? Did the same kind of mistake get a different response depending on who made it? Would you use the same words with someone else who did the same thing? If the answers are uneven, change the method. Offer coaching to everyone on a predictable basis. Use the same first question whenever work goes wrong: "What happened, and what do you need?"

Setbacks can be some of the best material for coaching. The Center for Creative Leadership's early research found that hardships were among the experiences leaders learned from. A 2020 CCL article reports that they were later dropped from the popular 70-20-10 guideline because organizations had little control over them. Treat it as a pointer from leadership research, not a rule. After a setback, ask what happened, what the person would do again, what they would do differently and what support was missing, including from you. Keep the talk on learning. Leave blame and repeated retelling out.

Some matters are not coaching matters. OPM's 2018 memo says coaching should not stand in for a supervisor's performance management duties. Consult Human Resources about performance responsibilities when needed; coaching is not a prerequisite for following a required procedure. Bring conduct, discipline and labor agreement questions to Human Resources and labor relations. Follow DHS complaint reporting procedures for discrimination, harassment or retaliation. Supervisors have additional immediate reporting and referral duties; do not wait for a coaching conversation to establish whether the concern is valid. Forward accommodation requests promptly under the agency's accommodation process, and tell the person who decides. Tell the person plainly that this part is now a different conversation. You can keep coaching on other goals.
